headline: New moon springs build toward a sunset flood window at Stepping Stones
subhead: Bass have been scattered and lockjawed on the slack tides all week, but bigger water arriving Friday through Monday should turn the lights back on at last light.
body_markdown:
Let me tell you what the last seven days felt like out here: warm, flat, and stingy. We came off the June full moon into a stretch of neap tides — small swings, weak current, water that just sat there instead of moving. Add in a run of light southwest wind and stable warm air, and you get exactly what I saw off Execution Rocks and the Stepping Stones light all week: bass that show for twenty minutes around the tide change and then vanish. When the current's soft, stripers don't have to commit. They can sit in the rockpiles and pick at whatever drifts by instead of setting up on a rip and feeding hard. That's been the story since last weekend — good marks on the machine, quiet rods.

That's about to change. We're building into a new moon, and the tides are already stacking bigger day over day. The real news for this zone is the PM flood window lining up with sunset from Friday the 10th through Monday the 13th, with the tightest alignment Saturday and Sunday. High stand at Kings Point is going to hit right around last light those two evenings, which is the exact recipe that turns Stepping Stones and the mouth of Manhasset Bay into a striper highway. Bigger spring tide, more water moving, current stacking bait against structure right as the light drops — that's when the bass that have been sulking all week get up on the reef and feed with some authority. If you've only got one evening to fish this month, Saturday or Sunday night on that incoming tide is the one I'd take.

In the meantime, the bite hasn't been dead, just honest work. Bass to 28 inches have been coming off Execution Rocks on the outgoing, fished tight to the rockpile in 15 to 20 feet with 1-ounce bucktails dressed in white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of fresh bunker belly. Slow-rolled right along the bottom edge where the rock drops into the channel — that's where they're sitting, using the structure to break the current and ambush whatever's getting swept through. A few guys working live eels after dark at the base of Hart Island have done well too, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping.

The bunker schools I told you to watch back in June are still stacked up off Matinecock Point, and they haven't thinned out much — pushed a little tighter to the beach with the warm water we've had. Where you find bunker balled up like that, bass and blues are shadowing them, especially at first light. Bluefish have actually been the more reliable player this week — 3- to 5-pound choppers blowing up on top off Matinecock and around the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings, chewing through anything metal. Diamond jigs in the 1- to 2-ounce range, or a topwater popper worked fast through the froth, and you're hooked up. That bite's been consistent morning and evening regardless of the tide funk, because blues don't care as much about current as bass do — they just want the bait ball.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, and here's why: the bay and harbor water has gotten warm — I've seen mid-to-upper 70s readings in the back harbors, Manhasset and Hempstead both — and that's pushed the better fluke out of the shallow bay water and into the deeper channels and toward the inlets where there's cooler water moving through. If you're drifting Little Neck Bay or the shallow flats and getting nothing but shorts, don't fight it — slide out to the channel edges and the mouth of Hempstead Harbor, work 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, and drag them slow on the last of the outgoing. That's where the keeper-class fish have been sitting, staged in the deeper cooler water waiting on bait to get pulled out of the bay with the tide.

Porgies have been steady and reliable, which is more than I can say for most everything else this week — Hart Island and the rockpiles off City Island are holding good numbers on bloodworms and squid strips, high-low rigs, fishing the bottom of the tide when the current eases up enough to keep bait on the hook. Blackfish season's closed in the Sound right now, so leave the tog gear home — those fish are off the menu until the fall opener.

And weakfish — I'll be straight with you, I haven't heard a single credible report out of this zone despite water temps that should be right for them. Warm water alone doesn't make weakfish show up; you need the bait and the right structure lining up too, and right now it just isn't happening here. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them specifically.

So here's my read heading into next week: the neap tide funk breaks as the new moon builds bigger water, and that PM flood window converging with sunset Friday through Monday is the best shot we've had since before the June full moon. I'd be at Stepping Stones or working the drift off Kings Point Saturday evening with bucktails and eels ready, watching that tide come up as the light drops. If the bass don't cooperate there, Matinecock's bunker schools are the fallback — where there's bait, there's usually something willing to eat it.
